title: Power outage
summary: Keep the food, medicine and phones safe while the lights are out.

items.text: List everything that runs on electricity, and plan batteries or a power bank for what matters.
Keep a flashlight for every household member.
Ask your medical provider for a plan for powered medical devices and refrigerated medicines.
items.note: Learn how long each medicine can tolerate higher temperatures. For insulin, see the guide.

items.text: Install carbon monoxide detectors with battery backup on every level.
Keep non-perishable food and water, plus coolers and a thermometer.
Find out where community locations with power are, and where heating or cooling sites open.

items.note: A fridge keeps food cold for about 4 hours. A full freezer holds for about 48 hours. Add ice to coolers if needed.

items.text: Run generators **outdoors only**, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages.
items.note: Keep it dry. Never run one indoors.

items.text: **Never heat the home with a gas stove or oven.**
items.note: Grills and camp stoves stay outdoors too.

items.text: Turn off or unplug appliances and electronics, to avoid damage from power surges.
Follow your plan for refrigerated medicines and powered medical devices.
If the heat or cold is extreme, go to a community location that has power.
items.note: Or go to Gram's, if that is the plan.

items.text: Stay at least 30 feet from downed power lines, treat them as live, and report them to the utility.
Throw out food that reached 40°F or higher for two hours or more, or that smells, looks or feels wrong.
items.note: When in doubt, throw it out.

items.text: If the outage lasted more than a day, discard refrigerated medicine unless its label says otherwise.
items.note: Insulin: read the insulin guide first. Call your doctor or pharmacist for a new supply.

items.text: Keep appliances disconnected until you have checked them, in case of power surges.
